title: CLAUDE.md
text:
This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.


This is a Quarto website project for a Year 1 Research Methods course (PS51020A) focusing on statistical analysis and research skills. The project uses Quarto with webR integration to create interactive educational content including lectures, labs, and data skills exercises.





# Render the entire website
quarto render

# Preview the website locally
quarto preview

# Render specific document
quarto render filename.qmd



The project uses the quarto-webr extension for interactive R code execution in browsers. WebR is configured globally in _quarto.yml and allows students to run R code without installing R locally.







Main Pages: index.qmd, lectures.qmd, labs.qmd, dataskills.qmd, r-resources.qmd
Weekly Content: Organized in folders like week01/, labs/, dataskills/
Demonstrations: demos/ folder contains various webR and Quarto feature examples
Worksheets: Student exercises in worksheets/ folder





Lecture Slides: RevealJS presentations (.qmd with format: revealjs)
Lab Materials: HTML documents with interactive R code blocks
Data Skills: Exercises combining theory and practice
Demonstrations: Feature showcases for code options, webR capabilities





quarto-webr: Enables interactive R code execution (_extensions/coatless/webr/)
downloadthis: Allows file downloads from web pages (_extensions/shafayetShafee/downloadthis/)





_quarto.yml: Main configuration with website structure, navigation, webR settings
styles.css: Custom styling
include/webex.css and include/webex.js: Interactive exercise components





Course data stored in appropriate weekly folders (e.g., week01/data/)
Research datasets typically in CSV format for R analysis




The website uses a combined navbar and sidebar structure: - Navbar: Main sections (Home, Lectures, Labs, DataSkills, R Resources) - Sidebar: Weekly content and demonstrations with automatic content discovery



WebR is configured to show minimal startup messages and is automatically attached to all pages via the filters section. This enables browser-based R code execution for educational content.

title: dataskills16
text:
Introduction
You are in charge of the selection procedure for a large company. For the past years, prospective new staff have participated in a recruitment exercise, in which a number of measures were taken which were thought to be important for the job. These include 4 paper and pencil tasks measuring verbal skills (verbal), spatial skills (spatial), number skills (number), and problem solving skills (problem), and 3 measures that are taken from observing the applicants during group exercises. These are social skills (social), motivation (motiv) and efficiency (effic). You have this information for 40 current staff, as well as their current job success (job), and their age when they took the tests.
Data is available in the file data/week16data.csv.

title: dataskills16
text:
Question
Do the assessment measures significantly predict job success? Which measures are particularly useful (significant)?

title: dataskills16
text:
Task
Run a multiple regression with the assessment measures as predictors and job success as the DV. Write this up in APA format, explaining what the results show. This should be in the format of a short results section.

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Lab Report Writing Skills
Workshop Objectives

Understand the structure of quantitative lab reports
Learn APA formatting for statistical results
Practice writing method and results sections
Apply multiple regression reporting guidelines

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Introduction to Quantitative Lab Reports
Purpose: Document empirical research in psychology
Key Features: - Systematic investigation of research questions - Statistical analysis of data - Clear communication of findings - Replicable methodology

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Example Study Context
Research Topic
Music Sophistication and Personality

Investigating relationships between musical engagement and personality traits
Using validated psychological measures
Applying multiple regression analysis

Measures Used

Gold-MSI: Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index
Big Five: Five-factor personality model (TIPI-10)

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Lab Report Structure
1. Title Page

Descriptive title
Author name(s)

Institutional affiliation
Author note

2. Abstract

Brief summary (150-250 words)
Research question, method, key findings
Conclusions and implications

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Method Section
Participants
Example: “A total of 156 undergraduate students (118 female, 38 male) participated in this study. Ages ranged from 18 to 24 years (M = 20.3, SD = 1.8). All participants were recruited from the university psychology participant pool and received course credit for participation.”
Materials
Describe each measure: - Gold-MSI (Müllensiefen et al., 2014) - 39-item measure of musical sophistication - Five subscales: Active Engagement, Perceptual Abilities, Musical Training, Singing Abilities, Emotions - 7-point Likert scale (1 = completely disagree, 7 = completely agree)

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Method Section (continued)
Procedure
Step-by-step description:

Participants accessed online survey via university portal
Informed consent obtained before data collection
Demographic information collected first
Gold-MSI questionnaire completed (10 minutes)
TIPI-10 personality measure completed (5 minutes)
Participants debriefed and thanked

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Results Section Structure
1. Descriptive Statistics

Means, standard deviations, ranges
Reliability coefficients (Cronbach’s α)
Sample characteristics

2. Preliminary Analyses

Assumption checking
Missing data handling
Outlier detection

3. Main Analyses

Statistical tests addressing research questions
Effect sizes and confidence intervals

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Writing Descriptive Statistics
Example Format
“Descriptive statistics for all measures are presented in Table 1. Musical sophistication scores ranged from 65 to 234 (M = 147.8, SD = 28.4), indicating substantial variability in musical engagement across participants.”
Reliability Reporting
“Internal consistency was acceptable for all scales: Gold-MSI total (α = .89), Extraversion (α = .68), Conscientiousness (α = .75), Emotional Stability (α = .73), Agreeableness (α = .40), Openness (α = .45).”

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Multiple Regression Reporting
Model Summary
“A multiple regression analysis was conducted to examine whether Big Five personality dimensions predicted musical sophistication scores. The overall model was statistically significant, F(5, 150) = 8.42, p < .001, and explained 22% of the variance in musical sophistication (R² = .22, adjusted R² = .19).”
Individual Predictors
APA Format: “Openness to Experience emerged as the strongest predictor (β = .35, t = 4.58, p < .001), followed by Extraversion (β = .28, t = 3.71, p < .001). Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Agreeableness were not significant predictors (all ps > .05).”

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Statistical Reporting Guidelines
Always Include:

Test statistic (t, F, r, etc.)
Degrees of freedom
Exact p-values (or p < .001)
Effect sizes (β, η², Cohen’s d)
Confidence intervals when available

Example:
Incorrect: “The correlation was significant (p < .05)” Correct: “Musical training was positively correlated with extraversion, r(154) = .34, p < .001, 95% CI [.19, .47]”

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Tables and Figures
Table Guidelines

Clear, informative titles
Appropriate number of decimal places
Consistent formatting
Notes explaining abbreviations

Figure Guidelines

Professional appearance
Clear axis labels
Appropriate scale
Caption explaining content

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Common Writing Issues
Avoiding Errors
❌ “The results were significant” ✅ “Musical training significantly predicted extraversion”
❌ “There was a correlation” ✅ “Musical training was positively correlated with extraversion”
❌ “The regression proved causation” ✅ “The regression analysis revealed significant associations”

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Discussion Section Tips
Structure:

Restate main findings in plain language
Interpret results in context of theory/literature

Acknowledge limitations of the study
Suggest future research directions
Conclude with practical implications

Avoid Over-interpretation

Correlation ≠ causation
Acknowledge alternative explanations
Be cautious about generalizability

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
Practical Exercise
Your Task
Using the multiple regression output provided:

Write a methods section describing the procedure
Report the overall model results in APA format
Describe individual predictor effects
Create a properly formatted results table

Dataset Context

Outcome: Job success ratings
Predictors: Verbal, spatial, numerical, problem-solving, social skills, motivation, efficiency
Sample: 40 current employees
Data Location: Available in the Week 16 DataSkills exercise

title: Week 16 Workshop: Lab Report Writing Skills
text:
APA Reference Examples
Journal Articles
Müllensiefen, D., Gingras, B., Musil, J., & Stewart, L. (2014). The musicality of non-musicians: An index for assessing musical sophistication in the general population. PLoS ONE, 9(2), e89642.
Book Chapters
Gosling, S. D., Rentfrow, P. J., & Swann, W. B. (2003). A very brief measure of the Big-Five personality domains. Journal of Research in Personality, 37(6), 504-528.

Lab reports follow standardized structure

Include all necessary statistical information

Tables and figures enhance understanding

Remember:

Precision in statistical reporting
Appropriate interpretation of findings
Professional writing style

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Interpreting (R), (R^2), and (R^2_{})

(R): correlation between observed and predicted (Y).

(R^2): variance explained (non‑decreasing as predictors are added).

(R^2_{}): penalises extra predictors: [ R^2_{} ;=; 1 - ]







Tip


Teaching move: Ask “What happens to (R^2) if we add a noise predictor?” Then show the static simulation plot below.

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Outline

Basics of multiple regression
Requirements
Reporting regression
Types of multiple regression

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Simple and Multiple Regression

Simple regression – predicting one variable (DV - Y) from another variable (IV - X)
Often more than one variable affects the DV
Multiple regression – predict Y from number of variables
More accurate prediction of Y

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple Regression

Goal of multiple regression – predict as much variance in DV as possible with fewest number of IVs
Each IV (predictor) accounts for unique amount of variance in DV
Multiple regression – most widely-used and most powerful statistical technique in psychology

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Requirements

Multiple regression has more stringent requirements than most other statistical methods
At least interval level measurement of DV
Sample size:

10 participants per IV is OK
20 is good

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Requirements
Normality and Linearity

variables must be normally distributed
variables should be linearly related to each other

Multicollinearity and Singularity

IVs must not be highly correlated with each other
Multi-collinearity – when \(r > 0.9\)
Singularity – when 2 variables are perfectly correlated

Example – you can’t use subscales of a test and the overall test score – the latter is an exact sum of the former

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Simple regression equation
\(Y = a + bX\)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression equation
\(Y = a + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + b_3X_3 + \ldots\)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression equation
Variable you want to predict (DV)
\(\mathbf{Y} = a + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + b_3X_3 + \ldots\)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression equation
Variable you want to predict (DV)
\(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{a} + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + b_3X_3 + \ldots\)
Constant

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression equation
Variable you want to predict (DV)
\(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b_1}X_1 + \mathbf{b_2}X_2 + \mathbf{b_3}X_3 + \ldots\)
Constant and Regression coefficients

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression equation
Variable you want to predict (DV)
\(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b_1}\mathbf{X_1} + \mathbf{b_2}\mathbf{X_2} + \mathbf{b_3}\mathbf{X_3} + \ldots\)
Constant, Regression coefficients, and Variables you know

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Output - R

R – strength of relationship between DV and combined set of IVs
Correlation between observed values of Y and values of Y predicted by multiple regression model
Index of how well the model predicts the observed data

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Output - R Square

\(R^2\) – variance accounted for – amount of variance in DV explained by IVs
Significance of \(R^2\) tested by ANOVA:

\(F = \frac{\text{Regression Mean Square (variance due to IVs)}}{\text{Residual Mean Square (error variance)}}\)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
R square

\(R^2\) gets larger every time another predictor is added to the model
New predictor may only provide a tiny improvement in amount of variance explained
\(R^2\) – not always useful – large set of predictors difficult to interpret
More predictors there are, the less reliable the results in terms of generalizing from the sample to the population.

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Adjusted R square

\(R^2_{adj}\) takes into account the number of predictors in the model
\(R^2\) is reduced according to the number of predictors in the model
Calculated as:

\(R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{(1-R^2)(N-1)}{(N-n-1)}\)
where:

\(N\) = number of participants
\(n\) = number of predictors

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Example

Predicting exam performance from IQ, number of lectures attended, revision time, and number of articles read in 40 students
\(R^2 = 0.6\) – so 60% of variance accounted for
4 predictors

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Example
\(R^2_{adj}\) – takes into account number of predictors (4)
\(R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{(1-R^2)(N-1)}{(N-n-1)}\)
\(= 1 - \frac{(1-0.6)(40-1)}{(40-4-1)}\)
\(= 1 - (0.4) \times \frac{39}{35} = 0.554\)
\(R^2_{adj} = 0.554\), so 55.4% of variance is explained

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Simple or multiple?

Depends on research question
Simple – basic questions
Less detail
Multiple –more depth
Explains more of the variance

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Reporting regression

Key information needed
Does the model as a whole significantly predict variance in the DV?
How much variance is explained (as % figure)
In a multiple regression – which predictors are significant

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Reporting regression
Does the model overall predict the DV – report the ANOVA
APA format: F(df1, df2) = F value, p = p value
The amount of variance explained:

\(R^2\) for simple regression
\(R^2_{adj}\) for multiple regression

Report as % (move decimal point 2 places to right)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Reporting regression

Which predictors are significant?
Look at the coefficients
Report t test to show significance
Report Beta values for comparison (Beta is standardised)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Types of multiple regression

Various types – looking at 4
Standard
Stepwise
Set-wise
Hierarchical

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Standard multiple regression

Also known as “Simultaneous Regression”
All predictor variables entered into regression model simultaneously in one step or block
Exploratory research – method to use

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Stepwise Regression

Also known as “Statistical Regression”
Order of entering variables based solely on statistical criteria
Use rarely and with extreme caution

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Stepwise regression - problems

\(R^2\) – badly biased high
Stepwise trawls through all variables that might be entered – capitalises on chance and inflates Type 1 error rate
p values are inaccurate and too low – may get false significant results
Relative importance of correlated IVs determined according to which enters first
Entry on first step based purely on which variable has numerically highest correlation with DV
Small differences in correlations likely to be caused by sampling error, unlikely to be replicable

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Stepwise regression - problems

Imagine sample 1 → DV, IV1, IV2
Correlations are:

DV and IV1 = 0.50
DV and IV2 = 0.49

On step 1, IV1 will automatically go in first, IV2 may well not enter later

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Stepwise regression - problems
Correlations are sample values that can show chance variation

Second sample:

DV and IV1 = 0.49
DV and IV2 = 0.50

IV2 would enter automatically first, and IV1 may not
Entry of IVs not reliable across samples

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Set-wise Regression

Sets of conceptually-related predictor variables entered together in each step
Example – predicting Job Satisfaction

Demographic variables
Personality variables
Job-related variables

These predictor variables would be entered as 3 separate sets

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Set-wise regression

Allows us to look at impact of one set of predictors
Changes when another set is added
Whether model is improved
How the variance explained changes

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Hierarchical regression

Used whenever there are good logical or theoretical reasons for a particular order
Predictor variables believed to have strongest influence on DV entered first
Also used when dealing with unwanted or ‘nuisance’ variables
Nuisance variables entered on first step to removed influence on DV

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Hierarchical regression

Example of method – prediction of voting behaviour, e.g. voting Labour, Conservative, LibDem, etc at next general election
Research has shown best predictor is past voting behaviour
Step 1: Past voting behaviour

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Hierarchical regression

Next best predictor might be voting intention
Past research has shown intention is a good predictor of actual behaviour
Step 1: Past voting behaviour
Step 2: Voting intention

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Hierarchical regression

3rd best predictor might be political attitude
Research has shown that left-wing vs right-wing or conservative vs liberal attitudes can predict voting behaviour
Step 1: Past voting behaviour
Step 2: Voting intention
Step 3: Political attitude

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Hierarchical regression

Next best predictor might be significant others
Research has shown people’s behaviour is affected by how they perceive behaviour of friends and family
Step 1: Past voting behaviour
Step 2: Voting intention
Step 3: Political attitude
Step 4: Significant others

…… and so on

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Hierarchical regression – nuisance variables

Looking at contribution of young children’s weight and height to their memory span
Age would be a nuisance variable – weight and height always increase with age in young children
Age entered on step 1 – to remove influence
Weight and height predictors entered on next steps

title: Webexercises
text: This set of exercises will test your knowledge about various aspects of deception in psychology. Answer the questions to check your understanding of key concepts, theories, and research findings in this area.

title: Webexercises
text:
Fill-In-The-Blanks

The tendency for people to believe they are less likely to be deceived than others is known as the  to deception.
In deception research, the  is an actor who works with the experimenter to deceive the actual participant.
The  is a genuine smile that involves both the mouth and the eyes, making it harder to fake in deceptive situations.

title: Webexercises
text:
Multiple Choice

Which of the following is NOT typically considered a reliable indicator of deception?


Increased blinking
Reduced hand gestures
Lack of eye contact
Increased speech errors

The theory that proposes that lying is more cognitively demanding than telling the truth is called:


Interpersonal Deception Theory
Cognitive Load Theory
Four-Factor Theory
Self-Presentation Theory

In a typical deception study, who is usually unaware of the true nature of the experiment?


Participant
Experimenter
Confederate
Research Assistant

title: Webexercises
text:
True or False

Polygraph tests are highly accurate and widely accepted in scientific communities as reliable lie detectors. 
TRUE
FALSE
People are generally better at detecting lies told by strangers than by those close to them. 
TRUE
FALSE
Microexpressions are brief, involuntary facial expressions that can potentially reveal concealed emotions in deceptive situations. 
TRUE
FALSE

title: Webexercises
text:
Longer MCQs
Which of the following best describes the “Truth-Default Theory” in deception research?

The theory that humans are naturally inclined to always tell the truthThe theory that humans tend to believe others are telling the truth unless given reason to think otherwiseThe theory that truth-telling is easier and requires less cognitive effort than lyingThe theory that cultural norms universally prioritize truthfulness over deception

What is the primary focus of Interpersonal Deception Theory (IDT)?

The neurological processes involved in creating and maintaining a lieThe psychological motivations that drive individuals to engage in deceptive behaviorThe dynamic interaction between the deceiver and the target of deceptionThe cultural variations in perceptions and acceptance of deceptive practices

title: Webexercises
text:
Checked sections

Research suggests that detecting deception is:

Easy for most people
Only possible with specialized training
Difficult, with accuracy rates often only slightly above chance
Impossible without technological aids
Explain why detecting deception is challenging for most people:


Click for explanation

Detecting deception is challenging for several reasons:

Many common beliefs about deception cues (e.g., lack of eye contact) are not reliable indicators.
Liars often strategically control their behavior to appear truthful.
Individual differences in baseline behavior make it hard to identify deviations.
The cognitive load of trying to detect lies can impair judgment.
Confirmation bias can lead people to interpret ambiguous cues in line with their expectations.

title: Webexercises
text:
Hidden solutions and hints
A researcher wants to study how cognitive load affects lying behavior. Describe a potential experimental design to investigate this.


I need a hint

Consider how you might manipulate cognitive load (e.g., through a secondary task) and measure lying behavior. Think about what control conditions you might need.




Click here to see a possible experimental design

# Possible Experimental Design:

# Participants: 100 adults randomly assigned to two groups (50 each)
# 
# Procedure:
# 1. All participants are asked to lie about a recent experience
# 
# 2. Experimental group: 
#    - Must count backwards from 100 by 7s while lying (high cognitive load)
# 
# 3. Control group:
#    - Simply lie without additional task (normal cognitive load)
# 
# 4. Measure dependent variables:
#    - Speech hesitations
#    - Speech rate
#    - Amount of detail provided
#    - Perceived believability (rated by independent judges)
# 
# 5. Compare measures between groups to assess the effect of cognitive load on lying behavior

# This design allows us to isolate the effect of increased cognitive load on various aspects of lying behavior.


This set of exercises covers various aspects of deception psychology, including theories, research methods, and key findings. It utilizes different question types to engage learners and test their understanding of the subject matter.
